prompt: A teammate opens an update with: "Over three weeks I pulled the event logs, reconciled them against billing, found duplicate charges, removed them, and re-ran the model." The actual news is that the revenue forecast dropped eight percent. Critique that opening.

criteria: Names that the eight percent drop arrives last instead of first
Says a reader may stop or be interrupted before reaching the news
Proposes a first line that leads with the forecast change
Keeps the reconciliation detail in the message rather than deleting it

prompt: The same finding can go into a memo the reader scrolls at their own pace, or into a live meeting where you may be interrupted at any moment. Where does putting the conclusion first matter more, and for what reason?

options: The meeting, because an interruption can arrive before you ever reach the conclusion
The meeting, because opening with the conclusion shortens the meeting
The memo, because the conclusion needs supporting sections stacked beneath it
Neither, because order changes how it feels but not what is understood

prompt: You have four pieces of a short update and thirty seconds of someone's attention. Put them in the order that survives being cut off halfway through.

items: How the estimate was produced, step by step
The answer: the pipeline can be ready by the 14th
The caveat you would raise only if asked
The two constraints that drive that date

prompt: A director messages you at 4:55pm: "Is the churn number in tomorrow's deck wrong?" It is — a filter dropped trial accounts and overstated churn by about three points. Write the reply you send.

criteria: Opens with the verdict — the number is wrong — in the first sentence
Gives the size or direction of the error before explaining the cause
Puts the filter problem after the answer, not as a preamble to it
Ends with what happens next and when a corrected figure arrives

prompt: The result of a pipeline migration has to go to the engineer who will maintain it and to the executive who funded it. Explain what you change between the two versions and what stays identical.

criteria: Names something the engineer already knows that the executive does not
States what each of the two will do with the information
Keeps the underlying finding and numbers the same in both versions
Names the executive's real worry — cost, risk, or timing — rather than assuming interest in mechanics

prompt: Match each reader of the same pipeline write-up to the thing they are actually worried about.

left: A finance partner reviewing your forecast
The on-call engineer inheriting the pipeline
A support lead whose team fields the complaints
An executive deciding whether to fund another quarter
right: What pages them at 3am, and how to make it stop
Whether the last quarter of spend produced anything
How many customers notice, and what to tell them
Whether the range is defensible enough to put in a budget

prompt: Before writing up a result, which questions actually tell you how to pitch it?

options: What will this person do with the answer once they have it?
What do they already know, so I am not re-explaining it?
What are they afraid is going wrong?
Which part of the work was the hardest to build?
Which chart style will look best on the slide?

prompt: Adjusting a message to its audience can slide into telling people what they want to hear. Where is the line, and how do you know when you have crossed it?

criteria: Separates changing the framing from changing the conclusion
Gives a case where an unwelcome finding has to survive the translation
Names what stays fixed no matter who is in the room
Offers a check for whether the message has been softened past the evidence

prompt: A fix you shipped changes a metric definition that three other teams quote in their own reporting. Beyond replying to the person who reported it, what does closing the loop require?

options: Nothing further — the person who reported it can pass the word along
Telling the teams who quote that metric what changed and from which date
Rebuilding every historical report yourself before saying anything to anyone
Waiting for someone to notice the discrepancy and then explaining the change

prompt: A colleague tells you that announcing your own finished work is self-promotion, and that the work should speak for itself. Argue against that.

criteria: Names who is left without information when nothing is announced
Points out that nobody outside the work can see that it finished
Separates reporting an outcome from claiming credit for it
Describes a low-cost form the announcement can take

prompt: True or false: if the person who requested a change has not chased it in a month, the change stopped mattering to them, so there is no need to tell them it shipped.

criteria: Says silence usually means they routed around the gap instead
Notes they may still be running a workaround built on the old behaviour
States the cost of sending the note as near zero either way
Points out the requester has no way to learn it shipped unless told
Says silence usually means they routed around the gap instead
Notes they may still be running a workaround built on the old behaviour
States the cost of sending the note as near zero either way
Points out the requester has no way to learn it shipped unless told

prompt: Six weeks ago someone reported that a report double-counted refunds. The fix went live this morning and nobody has asked about it since. Write the note you send them.

criteria: States in the first line that the fix is live
Says what the numbers show now that they did not before
Tells them whether figures they saved earlier have changed
Gives one concrete thing to look at or a way to reply

prompt: Fill in the blanks: a proposal that lists only upsides invites the reader to go hunting for the ______ you left out, while naming it yourself makes the proposal more ______.
A proposal reads, in full: "We should move the nightly refresh to hourly. Dashboards will be much fresher." Critique it as a recommendation.

criteria: Names that nothing is given up anywhere in the proposal
Identifies a specific cost such as compute spend, source load, or on-call burden
Argues the missing cost makes the proposal less credible rather than more persuasive
Sketches a version that states the cost in the same breath as the benefit

prompt: You want to cache an expensive join to cut a report's runtime, at the price of numbers that can be up to an hour stale. Put a number on what that hour of staleness costs, and show how you got there.

criteria: Gives a range instead of a single point figure
Names who is looking at the report during that stale hour
States the assumption the estimate rests on
Says what evidence would narrow the range

prompt: Which of these sentences actually name a tradeoff, rather than only advertising an upside?

options: Query cost drops by roughly half, and the figures can lag by up to an hour.
This is the strongest option on the table.
We get a same-day refresh; in exchange the team takes on a second on-call rotation.
It is faster, cheaper, and simpler than what we run today.
The model gets more accurate on new accounts and less accurate on the long tail.

prompt: You start ending every analysis with a firm recommendation instead of a menu of options. What breaks first, and who is the first to say something?

criteria: Names being wrong in public as the first thing that breaks
Gives a case where the decision-maker held context you did not
Says to attach the assumption or condition that would make the call falsifiable
Identifies who pushes back first and on what grounds

prompt: You send three options with pros and cons for each and no view of your own. What most often happens next?

options: The reader picks the same option you would have picked anyway
The decision stalls, or comes back to you asking which one you would choose
The reader values the neutrality and reaches a decision faster
The three options get merged into a fourth approach nobody costed

prompt: Arrange the four parts of a one-page memo whose job is to get a decision made, not to survey the field.

items: The alternatives you considered and why you set them aside
What would make you change your mind
The two reasons it beats the next-best option

prompt: Your manager asks for "a neutral summary of the three options, no recommendation — leadership will decide." You have a clear view on which option is right. How do you respond?

criteria: Names what the decision-makers lose without the view of the person closest to the data
Offers a form that still honours the request, such as options plus a stated lean
Says the recommendation can be labelled as one input, not as the decision
Avoids both silent compliance and a flat refusal to write it

prompt: A request lands as "need a churn number for the board deck by Thursday." A teammate replies "on it" and opens a query editor. Critique that response.

criteria: Names churn as undefined in the request as written
Points out the grain — accounts, seats, or revenue — was never specified
Notes that a board deck implies a comparison period nobody has agreed
States what the rework costs if the guess turns out wrong on Thursday

prompt: Someone drops into your channel with "can you send me last quarter's active users?" Before you write a line of SQL, what do you ask back, and what rework does each question prevent?

criteria: Asks what decision or artefact the number feeds
Asks when it is needed by
Asks about grain — active users counted per what
Pins down what counts as active before querying
Ties at least one question to specific rework it heads off

prompt: Match each intake question to the specific rework it prevents.

left: Counted per customer, per account, or per seat?
right: Stops the number being rebuilt later at a different grain
Stops a two-week build for a conversation happening tomorrow
Stops two teams quoting different figures for the same word
Stops a precise answer to a question nobody was asking

prompt: A stakeholder asks for "revenue by region for the last year." Which follow-ups are worth asking before you start building?

options: Bookings or recognised revenue?
Region by billing address or by sales territory?
Calendar year, or the trailing twelve months?
Would you prefer a bar chart or a line chart?
Should I write it as a CTE or a subquery?

prompt: A teammate's weekly update reads in full: "Still deep in the pipeline refactor. Lots of moving parts, more complex than expected. Will keep everyone posted." Critique it as the person who has to decide whether to move a launch date.

criteria: Points out that no finished piece of work is named
Notes there is no next step with a date attached
Says whether anything is blocked is left unanswered
Names the reader's actual question: does the date still hold

prompt: Sort each line from a weekly update into the section a reader expects to find it under.

left: The backfill finished Tuesday and the monthly totals reconcile
I pick up the deduplication logic on Monday
Sitting on a credential request with the platform team since Wednesday

prompt: You spent the whole week waiting on access to a source system and nothing else moved. What belongs in this week's update?

options: Nothing — skip the update, since there is no progress to report
The blocker, who can clear it, and what slips if it is not cleared
A detailed plan for the work you will start once access arrives
A one-line note that it was a quiet week

prompt: Your manager asks you to drop the short Friday note and send one detailed summary at the end of each month instead, because the weekly ones are "a lot of email". Write your reply.

criteria: Names cadence rather than length as the thing being given up
States that a month is too late for a blocker to surface
Grants something real about the manager's objection
Ends on a specific alternative rather than only an objection
